subsection: 5. Voluntary and statutory consumer protection bodies

notes.b: When something goes wrong as a consumer, there are two kinds of organisation that can help. Consumer protection bodies are either established by law with legal powers, or operate voluntarily through advice, research and self-regulation.
points: Statutory bodies are established by an Act of the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament) and are funded by the State. They have legal powers to investigate, enforce and, in some cases, prosecute.
Voluntary bodies are independent or industry-based. They advise, research, lobby and handle complaints, but they have no legal powers, so they cannot compel a trader to act.
Self-regulation means an industry sets its own standards. For example, the advertising industry sets its own code, and a voluntary body handles public complaints made under that code.

A consumer with a complaint about a trader should usually approach the trader first, because most problems are settled at that stage. If that fails, use the statutory or voluntary body that fits the problem.
notes.tip: If asked to name a statutory or a voluntary body, name one in the correct class and give its role. Full marks need the full name plus two points of role, in separate sentences.

notes.b: The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) is the state body that enforces consumer law. It was established by statute in 2014 and took over the work of the National Consumer Agency and the Competition Authority.
points: It enforces the Consumer Protection Act 2007 and other consumer law, so it acts on behalf of all consumers through the law.
It investigates unfair and illegal trading practices, including false or misleading advertising and pricing, such as a price that is not what the trader claims.
It can prosecute offences under consumer law, which is a legal power that voluntary bodies do not have.
It informs consumers of their rights through its website and helpline, and runs consumer information campaigns, including on personal finance.
It enforces product-safety rules for non-food products, which protects consumers from unsafe goods.
It promotes competition and advises government on consumer issues.
It does not resolve individual disputes between a consumer and a trader; it deals with breaches of the law and with information for consumers.
notes.tip: For 'name and give details of one statutory agency', the CCPC works well: give enforcement, investigation, information, non-food product safety and advice to government. Give the ASA as complaint handling, never prosecution, but the CCPC can prosecute.

notes.h: Citizens Information and the Citizens Information Board (statutory)
notes.b: Citizens Information provides free, confidential information and advice on rights and entitlements, including consumer rights. The Citizens Information Board is the statutory body behind it.
points: The Citizens Information Board is a statutory body that funds and supports (oversees) Citizens Information Centres and services.
Citizens Information Centres are local, independent services that give free, confidential information on consumer issues, so a consumer can get advice face to face.
Services cover consumer issues, social welfare entitlements, housing, health and other rights.
The Citizens Information website and phone service give access to information on rights from anywhere in Ireland, so a consumer does not have to visit a centre.
notes.tip: A common question asks for two functions of the Citizens Information Board. Give free and confidential information on rights and entitlements, and funding and supporting local centres, or the phone service and website. Do not put the Board under voluntary.

notes.h: Office of the Ombudsman and Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (statutory)
notes.b: An ombudsman is an independent official who investigates complaints that have not been resolved directly with the body concerned. Ireland has two that matter to consumers, one for public bodies and one for financial providers.
points: The Office of the Ombudsman investigates complaints about the administrative actions of public bodies, such as government departments, the HSE and local authorities.
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO) investigates complaints about financial service providers, such as banks, insurers, credit unions and pension providers.
The FSPO replaced the Financial Services Ombudsman and the Pensions Ombudsman in 2018, so one office now covers both areas.
Both are a last resort: the consumer must first use the provider's or body's own complaints procedure, and only then go to the ombudsman.
Investigations are free of charge to the complainant.
notes.tip: Matching questions pair a bank or insurer complaint with the provider first and then the FSPO, and a public service complaint with the Office of the Ombudsman. Neither deals with a faulty product from a shop.

notes.b: The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) protects consumers from food-related risks. It is the body to turn to for unsafe or mislabelled food.
points: It was established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, which is why it counts as a statutory body.
It sets and monitors food safety standards and gives consumers advice on food.
It works with official control agencies, such as the HSE and local authorities, that inspect food businesses on its behalf.
notes.tip: The FSAI is one of the statutory bodies accepted when you are asked to name three, so give its full name and one role.

notes.h: Other statutory bodies accepted in exams
notes.b: Marking schemes accept a few more statutory bodies, each protecting consumers in a particular area. Know the full name and one role for each.
points: The Central Bank of Ireland regulates financial service providers and protects consumers of financial services.
The National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) sets and certifies standards, so consumers can trust that products meet an agreed standard.

European Consumer Centre Ireland advises consumers on cross-border purchases within the EU, such as faulty goods bought online from a trader in another EU country. It is run by the CCPC as part of an EU network.
The small claims procedure is a court route for settling a dispute, not a consumer protection body, so it is not the answer to a question that asks for a body.
notes.tip: Name three statutory bodies from the CCPC, Office of the Ombudsman, FSAI, Citizens Information Board, Central Bank, NSAI and European Consumer Centre. Schemes list European Consumer Centre Ireland as statutory or voluntary, so always give its role.

notes.b: The Consumers' Association of Ireland (CAI) is an independent, non-profit organisation that represents consumers. It was founded in 1966.
points: It researches and tests goods and services and publishes its findings in Consumer Choice, so consumers can compare products before buying.
It provides objective information and advice on consumer products and services, including a personal advisory service.
It lobbies government on consumer issues, meaning it presses for changes that favour consumers.
It represents consumers on a number of bodies, so consumers have a voice where decisions are made.
notes.tip: For the role of the CAI, give researching and testing, publishing in Consumer Choice, objective advice, and lobbying and representing consumers. Do not put the CAI under statutory.

notes.b: The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) is a self-regulatory body for advertising, set up by the advertising industry itself. Older material calls it the Advertising Standards Authority for Ireland (ASAI).
points: It promotes high standards in advertising through a code, requiring that advertisements are legal, decent, honest and truthful.
It investigates complaints from the public about advertisements, such as false claims or offensive content.
Where a complaint is upheld, the advertiser is asked to amend or withdraw the advertisement. The ASA has no legal powers, so it relies on the industry complying with the code.
notes.tip: The CCPC enforces the law; the ASA enforces a code of its own industry. Describe the ASA as complaint handling and self-regulation, not prosecution, and write that it asks advertisers to amend or withdraw.

notes.b: Some voluntary help comes from industry groups and local services rather than from a single national organisation.
points: Trade associations look after the interests of their members and may have codes of practice and complaints procedures, so a consumer can complain to the association about a member.
Citizens Information Centres, as local services, are accepted as voluntary in some schemes because they are staffed partly by volunteers.

notes.h: Matching the body to the problem
notes.b: Exam questions often describe a problem and ask which body helps. Work out whether the problem is about the law, a code, money, public services, food or a purchase from abroad.
points: A misleading price or advertising claim goes to the CCPC (which enforces the law) or the ASA (which enforces the advertising code).
A complaint about a bank or insurer goes to the provider first, then to the FSPO.
A complaint about a public service goes to the Office of the Ombudsman.
To find consumer information, use Citizens Information, the CCPC or the CAI.
Faulty goods from an EU trader bought online go to European Consumer Centre Ireland.
Unsafe or mislabelled food goes to the FSAI.
notes.tip: Matching questions pair a bank complaint with the FSPO and an advert with the ASA. Statutory and voluntary are the two classes asked, so give the body in the correct class.

keyTerms.definition: A body established by law with legal powers to investigate, enforce and in some cases prosecute.
An independent or industry-based body that advises, researches and lobbies, without legal power to compel a trader.
The practice by which an industry sets and polices its own standards, often through a code.
Putting the case for consumers to government so that policy and law reflect consumer interests.
Bringing a criminal case against a trader for an offence under consumer law.
An organisation of businesses in one sector that protects its members' interests and sets their standards.
Written rules of conduct that an industry or association agrees to follow.
The final step in a complaints process, reached only after the trader or provider has been given a chance to resolve the matter.

factCards.term: Three functions of the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
factCards.definition: Enforces consumer law and investigates unfair or illegal trading practices; informs consumers of their rights; advises government on consumer issues.
Free, confidential information on rights and entitlements, and advice on consumer issues.

factCards.term: Role of the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
factCards.definition: Investigates complaints about financial service providers, as a last resort after the provider's own complaints process.

factCards.term: Two functions of the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland
factCards.definition: Promotes legal, decent, honest and truthful advertising; investigates public complaints and asks the advertiser to amend or withdraw an advertisement.

factCards.term: Three activities of the Consumers' Association of Ireland
factCards.definition: Researches goods and services and publishes findings; provides objective information and advice; lobbies government on consumer issues.

factCards.term: Main difference between legally established and advisory consumer organisations
factCards.definition: Legally established bodies have statutory powers to investigate and enforce; advisory bodies rely on research, advice and self-regulation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a statutory body and a voluntary body concerned with consumer protection, naming one of each.
questions.model: Statutory body: set up by law, with legal powers to investigate, enforce and prosecute; for example the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission. Voluntary body: independent or industry-based, offering advice, research, lobbying and complaint handling, but with no power to compel a trader to act; for example the Consumers' Association of Ireland or the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland. Other correct names are acceptable, provided the distinction in legal powers is made.

questions.prompt: Discuss the role of at least three bodies, statutory and voluntary, that help a consumer who has a complaint about an advertisement or a faulty service.
questions.model: Advertisement: the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland, a voluntary self-regulatory body, investigates public complaints about false, misleading or offensive advertising and can require changes or withdrawal of the advertisement. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, a statutory body, investigates misleading advertising and pricing and can prosecute offences under the Consumer Protection Act 2007. Faulty service or goods: Citizens Information, a statutory service through the Citizens Information Board, gives free, confidential advice on rights and how to complain. The Consumers' Association of Ireland, a voluntary body, gives objective advice and represents consumers. For a complaint against a financial service provider, the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman investigates as a last resort. A complete answer distinguishes the legal powers of statutory bodies from the advice and self-regulation offered by voluntary bodies.
